description: Antidepressants, CBT, reductionist vs holistic perspectives, and Wiles' CBT effectiveness study.
content_html:
Treating Depression: Two Main Approaches

The spec identifies two main interventions for depression: biological and psychological. The choice of treatment often reflects the theory of what causes depression — biological treatments target brain chemistry, while psychological treatments target thought patterns. In practice, a combination of both is often recommended.

Antidepressant Medications

Antidepressant medications work by altering the chemistry of the brain to reduce the symptoms of depression. The most widely prescribed type in the UK are SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors). SSRIs work by blocking the reuptake of serotonin into the pre-synaptic neuron after it has crossed the synapse — leaving more serotonin available to continue stimulating the post-synaptic neuron. This increases serotonin activity in the brain, which is associated with improved mood.

Antidepressants are prescribed by a doctor, take several weeks to have their full effect, and typically need to be taken daily. They reduce the chemical symptoms of depression, which can make it easier for a person to engage in psychological therapies or resume normal functioning. However, they do not address the underlying thought patterns that may have contributed to depression.

Key Fact

Antidepressants (especially SSRIs) treat depression by blocking serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonin availability at the synapse. This is a biological, reductionist intervention targeting brain chemistry directly.

Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT)

Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT) is a psychological talking therapy. It is based on the idea that depression is maintained by negative thought patterns (the cognitive element) and the behaviours that follow from them (the behavioural element). By identifying and challenging these patterns, a person can change how they think and behave, which in turn improves their mood.

In CBT sessions, a therapist works collaboratively with the client to identify automatic negative thoughts — patterns of thinking such as overgeneralising, catastrophising or personalising failure. The therapist then uses techniques such as cognitive restructuring (examining evidence for and against a negative thought) and behavioural activation (gradually reintroducing activities the person has withdrawn from) to build healthier patterns.

Antidepressants represent a reductionist approach: they reduce the treatment of depression to a single causal mechanism — a chemical imbalance in the brain — and correct it with medication. This has the advantage of being straightforward and evidence-based, but it ignores the wider context of the person’s life, relationships and thought patterns.

CBT represents a more holistic approach: it treats the person as a whole, addressing not just the symptoms but the thought patterns, behaviours and coping strategies that maintain depression. However, it requires significant engagement and effort from the client and may not be suitable for everyone, particularly those with severe depression.

Key Fact

Antidepressants = reductionist (target brain chemistry alone). CBT = holistic (addresses thoughts, behaviours and the whole person). The spec expects you to apply these terms to evaluate both treatments.

Aim: Wiles and colleagues aimed to investigate whether adding CBT to usual antidepressant medication improved outcomes for patients with treatment-resistant depression (patients whose symptoms had not improved with antidepressants alone).

Method: Participants were patients who had not responded to antidepressant treatment. They were assigned to one of two conditions: continuing antidepressants as usual, or continuing antidepressants plus receiving CBT sessions. Symptoms were measured at regular intervals over a follow-up period.

Results: Those who received CBT in addition to their medication showed greater improvement in depressive symptoms than those who received medication alone. A significantly higher proportion of the CBT group showed a meaningful reduction in symptoms.

Conclusion: CBT is an effective additional treatment for depression, even when antidepressants alone have not worked. This supports a combined (holistic) approach to treatment rather than relying solely on medication.

Evaluating the Therapies

Both therapies have strengths. Antidepressants typically take 2–6 weeks to have their full effect — faster than a complete course of CBT, but not quick in absolute terms. They are widely accessible (a GP can prescribe them without a long waiting list) and can be taken independently. CBT has long-lasting effects because it teaches skills the person can use independently — it does not just treat symptoms but addresses underlying patterns. Wiles’ study provides good evidence that the two can work together effectively.

Weaknesses also exist. Antidepressants can have side effects and do not address thought patterns — depression may return when medication is stopped. CBT is resource-intensive, requires a willing and engaged client, and may have a waiting list on the NHS. Neither treatment is effective for every person.
exam_tip_html: For Wiles’ study, make sure you can give the full AMRC: aim (CBT added to antidepressants for treatment-resistant patients), method (two conditions: medication only vs medication + CBT), results (CBT group showed greater improvement), conclusion (CBT is effective even when medication alone has not worked). When evaluating therapies, use the words “reductionist” and “holistic” explicitly — the mark scheme looks for these terms in extended answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Antidepressants (especially SSRIs) treat depression by blocking serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonin at the synapse. This is a reductionist, biological approach.
  • CBT is a holistic talking therapy that identifies and challenges negative thought patterns and unhelpful behaviours, building skills the person can use independently.
  • Wiles’ study found that adding CBT to antidepressant medication produced significantly greater improvement in treatment-resistant patients, supporting a combined approach.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes how SSRIs work to treat depression?
A) They increase the production of new neurons in the hippocampus
B) They block serotonin reuptake, increasing its availability at the synapse
C) They suppress the activity of the sympathetic nervous system
D) They stimulate the production of dopamine in the frontal lobe
practice_questions.marks: B) They block serotonin reuptake, increasing its availability at the synapse [1 mark]

Mastering: Definition states CBT is a talking therapy AND that it helps people identify and change negative thought patterns and the behaviours that maintain depression — both elements clearly expressed.
Secure: Both elements present but one vague.
Developing: Mentions talking or changing thoughts but without both elements of the full definition.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a reductionist and a holistic approach to treating depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. Students should: define reductionist as explaining/treating depression through a single, simpler mechanism (biology/brain chemistry) (1); define holistic as treating the whole person including thoughts, behaviour and social context (1); apply these terms to antidepressants (reductionist) and CBT (holistic) (1).
Mastering: Both terms defined and correctly applied to a specific treatment each.
Secure: Both terms defined, one applied.
Developing: One term defined with application.
Emerging: Vague description of the difference without using the correct terms.

practice_questions.text: Explain how CBT helps to improve mental health in people with depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the core mechanism (challenges negative automatic thoughts); explains the cognitive element (restructuring thought patterns) and behavioural element (reintroducing avoided activities); explains why this improves mood (thinking and behaviour change creates a positive cycle). Two developed points.
Secure: Identifies negative thought patterns as the target and explains at least one technique.
Developing: States that CBT helps people think differently but without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague reference to talking helping or thinking being changed.

practice_questions.text: Describe Wiles' study of the effectiveness of CBT, including the aim, method, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for: aim (to investigate whether CBT added to antidepressants improved outcomes for treatment-resistant patients); method (two conditions — medication as usual vs medication plus CBT; symptoms measured over time); results (CBT group showed significantly greater improvement than medication-only group); conclusion (CBT effective even when medication alone has not worked); implication (supports a combined/holistic treatment approach).
Mastering: All five elements.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to CBT working without AMRC structure.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the use of antidepressants and CBT as treatments for depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of both treatments (how SSRIs work, what CBT does); identifies reductionist/holistic perspectives; uses Wiles' study as evidence for CBT; two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. antidepressants don't address thought patterns — depression may return; CBT teaches lasting skills but is resource-intensive), each developed with reasoning.
Secure: Both treatments described; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One treatment described in detail; one evaluative point.
Emerging: Vague description of both; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Wiles' study found that adding CBT to medication was most helpful for which group of patients?
options: Patients whose symptoms had not improved with antidepressants alone

knowledge_checks.q: Antidepressants treat depression by blocking serotonin _____, leaving more serotonin available in the synapse.
CBT is described as a _____ approach to treating depression because it treats the whole person, not just brain chemistry.
Match each treatment to the perspective it best represents.
right: Combination of reductionist and holistic elements

flashcard_questions.a: They block serotonin reuptake, leaving more serotonin active at the synapse.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is antidepressant medication described as a reductionist treatment?
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces depression to a chemical imbalance and treats only that, ignoring wider factors.

flashcard_questions.q: What is CBT, and what does it target?
flashcard_questions.a: A talking therapy that identifies and changes negative thought patterns and behaviours.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is CBT described as a holistic treatment?
flashcard_questions.a: It treats the whole person — thoughts, behaviours and coping strategies, not just symptoms.

flashcard_questions.q: What are automatic negative thoughts in CBT?
flashcard_questions.a: Habitual pessimistic thoughts that distort perception of oneself, the world and the future.
Whether adding CBT to antidepressants improved outcomes for treatment-resistant patients.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Wiles find in her study?
flashcard_questions.a: CBT added to medication produced greater symptom improvement than medication alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Wiles' conclusion about the effectiveness of CBT?
flashcard_questions.a: CBT is effective even when antidepressants alone have not worked.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one strength of antidepressant medication as a treatment.
flashcard_questions.a: It is widely accessible and effective for many people, with relatively quick onset.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of CBT as a treatment for depression.
flashcard_questions.a: It requires motivation and effort from the client and may not suit severe depression.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why CBT may have more lasting effects than antidepressants.
flashcard_questions.a: CBT teaches skills the person keeps using after treatment ends; medication doesn't.

glossary_terms.definition: Treatments or therapies designed to reduce the symptoms of a mental health condition and improve a person's psychological wellbeing.
Medications prescribed to relieve symptoms of depression, typically by increasing the availability of neurotransmitters such as serotonin in the brain.
A talking therapy that helps people identify and change negative thought patterns (cognitions) and the unhelpful behaviours that maintain depression.
Automatic negative thoughts that occur without conscious effort and distort perception of oneself, the world and the future.
An approach that explains complex behaviour by breaking it down to its simplest parts, typically biological or physiological processes.
An approach that considers the whole person, including biological, psychological, social and environmental factors, rather than reducing behaviour to a single cause.
